studies.didYouKnow: The verb for varying the warnings occurs six times in the Quran, and a related form is used twice for the shifting of the winds. The word for being shortchanged in the line before it appears nowhere else in the text. A recurring word and a unique one sit in consecutive ayat, and both are about exactness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a claim about how revelation works. Warnings are varied rather than repeated because people are reached differently, and the aim is stated twice in weakening terms, first as becoming mindful and then as merely producing a lesson. That modest second hope is honest about what a text can do. Alongside it, the guarantee against quiet reduction says that the accounting will be exact where human accounting usually is not.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for varying the message in this Quran, and notes it increases some only in aversion.
Describes it as an Arabic recitation with no crookedness in it, so that people might be mindful.
Gives the instruction that follows this self-description, not to hurry with the revelation being received.

studies.applyIt: Notice the smaller of the two promises. Not being wronged is easy to want; not being quietly shortchanged is the one you feel in ordinary life, in the credit that goes elsewhere and the effort nobody sees. Bring one of those to mind today and let it go unclaimed, on the understanding that the measure it belongs to is exact.

studies.title: Increase Me In Knowledge
studies.meaning: Three movements in one ayah. God is declared exalted as the true King, which closes the scene of judgement just described. Then an instruction about receiving revelation: do not hurry it before its conveying to you is completed, which the commentators connect to repeating the words while they were still arriving. Then a prayer of three words, and it names the one thing the messenger is instructed to ask for more of.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah follows a passage on the Day of Resurrection and precedes the account of Adam's forgetting, so it sits between two scenes about what human beings do not hold onto. Classical reports say the instruction about haste concerns the practice of moving the tongue along with the revelation as it came, out of fear of losing it. A parallel instruction appears in a short surah.

keyTerms.note: A verb for wanting something before its time. It is used elsewhere in the Quran of people demanding punishment early, so the same impulse is being addressed in a much gentler setting.
A verb of finishing and settling, used of a debt paid off and a matter decided. The condition is that the revelation has finished arriving, not that it has been understood.

An imperative followed by an indefinite noun, so what is asked for is unmeasured knowledge rather than a particular subject. The brevity is part of why the phrase has been carved above libraries for centuries.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Learning in that world meant sitting with someone and holding what they said. There were no notes to check afterwards and no way to look a thing up, so a student's whole method was attention followed by repetition. Hurrying a teacher was the classic beginner's error, and every reciter knew what it cost: you kept the first half and lost the second. The instruction here describes a familiar failure.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer is three words in Arabic and is among the most quoted phrases in the language, appearing on university seals, library doors and certificates across the Muslim world. Commentators have long noted that it is the one place where the instruction is to ask for more of something rather than for pardon, guidance or protection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two halves are joined by a shared subject: how a person receives what is given. The instruction is to stop grasping at the revelation before it has finished coming, and the prayer is to be given more. Wanting more and grabbing at it are separated, which is a fine distinction and a useful one. It also establishes that a person who has been given revelation directly is still told to ask for more knowledge, which sets no ceiling anywhere below that.

crossReferences.why: The parallel instruction not to move the tongue in haste, with the same reassurance.
Says God raises in rank those given knowledge among the believers.
Above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows more.

studies.applyIt: Ask one question today that you have been avoiding because asking it would show you do not already know. To a colleague, a teacher, your own child. Say the three words of this prayer first if it helps. The ayah pairs not rushing with asking for more, and the second is impossible without admitting the gap.

studies.title: But He Forgot
studies.meaning: The surah opens its last narrative with a diagnosis rather than a scene. A covenant was made, it was forgotten, and no firm resolve was found in him. Commentators read the second clause as explaining the first: what failed was not intention but the holding of it. Only then does the story begin, with the angels told to bow and one refusal recorded in a single word. The order puts human forgetting before any account of temptation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just described the last day and now turns to the first. Its audience knew the outline of this story from the Jewish and Christian communities of Arabia, and the Quran's telling is deliberately compressed, keeping the covenant, the forgetting and the refusal. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The placement, at the end of a surah about a people who could not wait forty nights, carries the argument.

keyTerms.note: The same root used earlier in this surah when Moses asks whether the covenant had grown long for his people. One word covers an undertaking and the time that passes while it is meant to hold.
Forms of this verb run through the surah. God is said not to forget, the people claim Moses forgot, and here the first human being does. It is the surah's recurring word for how things go wrong.
This exact form occurs only here. It names the steadiness that holds a decision in place over time, so what is missing is not good intent but the grip that keeps it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agreements in Arabia lived or died on memory. There were no registries and few written contracts, so a pact of protection or a debt was fixed by witnesses, a public formula and sometimes a knotted cord, and the parties rehearsed it aloud so that others could recall it later. Forgetting an undertaking was not a private lapse. It dissolved the only record that existed.
studies.didYouKnow: Forms of the verb to forget appear in four separate ayat of this surah. Early on, Moses says his Lord neither errs nor forgets. The people say Moses forgot. Here the first human being forgets, and near the surah's end a person is told he forgot the signs that came to him. One failing is traced from God's exemption through a whole history.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the original human problem in memory rather than in appetite or pride. That is a gentler diagnosis than it first appears, since forgetting is treated as a condition to be worked against rather than a crime. It also sets up the contrast the surah has been building: the one who never forgets, and the creature whose covenant needs constant renewal because holding anything steadily is the thing he cannot do.

crossReferences.why: States earlier in this surah that God neither goes astray nor forgets, the exact counterpart to this failure.
Gives the same instruction to the angels and the same refusal, with pride named as the reason.
Narrates what follows the covenant, the whispering about the tree and the loss of the garden.

studies.applyIt: Take one commitment you made and quietly dropped, not from a change of mind but because it slipped. Do not renew it with a bigger promise. Instead attach it to something that already happens daily, a meal, a commute, a prayer, so that the remembering is not left to you. The passage says resolve, not sincerity, is what was missing.

studies.title: This Is An Enemy
studies.meaning: The warning is given before anything happens, and it is specific. The enemy is identified, the two people at risk are named together, and the danger is described as expulsion rather than as sin. Then the consequence is put in one word about hardship, and the grammar addresses it to Adam alone even though both were warned. Commentators note the shift, reading it as responsibility resting on the one who was told, without lifting it from the other.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has moved from its account of the last day to the first human story, and it tells it briefly, keeping the warning, the whisper and the outcome. Its Meccan listeners were themselves being warned repeatedly and watching the warnings ignored. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah; the surah is placing an old pattern beside a present one.

keyTerms.note: From a root for running past a limit or crossing over. An enemy in Arabic is one who transgresses against you, so the word describes a relation of hostility rather than a category of being.
The verb is dual, addressed to two people equally, and it puts the danger in terms of losing a place. Nothing is said yet about a forbidden act, only about being got out of somewhere.
A word for wretchedness and hard labour together, the opposite of ease rather than of happiness. The following ayat unpack it into four specific hardships.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion from a settled place was the recognised catastrophe of Arabian life. A clan driven from its wells and palm groves became dependent on the hospitality of others, and poets recorded such reversals for generations. The listeners in Mecca included people whose families had been pushed out of Yathrib or Yemen within living memory, and some of them would themselves emigrate before the surah was many years old.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for suffering is picked up again six ayat later, at the end of the same episode, where those who follow guidance are promised they will not go astray and will not suffer. The surah takes the exact term from the warning and turns it into the reassurance, so the whole story runs between one word and its cancellation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The danger is named before it arrives, which sets a pattern the Quran keeps: warning precedes trial, so failure is never a matter of not having been told. It is also striking that the harm identified is not divine anger but hardship, described in terms of the body's needs. The passage treats the loss as a change of condition rather than as a punishment inflicted from outside.

crossReferences.why: Answers this warning six ayat later, promising that whoever follows the guidance will not suffer.
Recalls the same warning after the fact, God asking whether He had not told them of that enemy.
States the relation generally, that the enemy is an enemy and should be treated as one.

studies.applyIt: Notice how early the warning comes. Think of one thing you already know is a problem for you, and that you have been told about, perhaps more than once. Write the warning down in your own words today. Not a plan, not a promise. Just the sentence, in the form you would need to hear it in.

studies.title: Four Things You Will Not Feel
studies.meaning: The garden is defined entirely by absences, and they come in two pairs. Hunger with nakedness, then thirst with exposure to the sun. Commentators note the pairing joins what the body needs inside with what it needs against the weather, so the four together cover every physical want. Against that completeness the whisper offers two things nobody had said were missing: a tree that confers permanence, and a rule that does not wear out.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran gives this episode in several surahs with different emphases; this telling is the only one that lists the four securities. The audience lived in a valley without agriculture, dependent on trade and on water from a single well, where the four needs named here were the daily arithmetic of survival. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb for the specific thirst of a body without water, not for wanting a drink. In a desert vocabulary it is the most serious of the four words, and it is placed third rather than first.
To be exposed to the full sun with no shade. The word occurs only here, and it shares its root with the term for the bright late morning, which the surah used earlier for the hour of the contest.
Not simply long life but continuance without end. The whisper attaches it to a tree, and pairs it with rule that does not decay, so both offers are about time rather than pleasure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no crops. Food came in by caravan, water came from wells that were guarded and allocated, and the valley's heat between the black hills was severe enough that shade was a form of property. Clothing was expensive and often the largest thing a poor family owned. The four things named here were not abstractions to that audience; they were the four ways a person died.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran that lists the garden's securities as four denials, and the last of the four words appears nowhere else in the text. Its root is the same one that gives the name of a short late surah and the hour of bright morning light, which this same surah used earlier for the time Moses set for the contest.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Temptation is shown working on someone who lacks nothing. Every physical need has just been declared met, and the offer that succeeds is not for food or comfort but for permanence and a dominion that does not decay. The passage locates the human vulnerability past the body, in the wish not to end, which is why satisfying needs has never by itself protected anyone from wanting more.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same whisper with a different offer, that eating would make them angels or immortals.
Uses the same root earlier in this surah for the bright morning hour Moses chose for the public contest.
Names the one who whispers into the breasts of people, using the same verb as the next ayah here.

studies.applyIt: Take stock the way the ayat do. Name, in order, whether you are hungry, clothed, thirsty and out of the weather right now. Almost certainly all four are fine. Then notice what you were worrying about before you read this. The distance between those two lists is the subject of this passage.

studies.title: Then His Lord Chose Him
studies.meaning: The act takes half a line and its consequences take the rest. What became visible was not a new thing but something they had not been aware of, and the first response was to cover it with what was to hand. Then the verdict is stated plainly, in two words that the Quran does not soften. The next ayah answers with three verbs in a row, and the first of them is not forgiveness but selection: he was chosen, then pardoned, then guided.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Surah 20 tells this episode in a handful of ayat where other surahs take longer, and it is the only telling that places the choosing before the pardon. The Meccan community included people who had done things they believed disqualified them, and the surahs of this period return often to the question of whether a fall is final. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb from cobbling, the stitching of one layer of leather onto another. It is used of these two in only one other place, and it makes the covering look improvised rather than dignified.
A verb for losing the right course through error rather than defiance. The Quran states it without qualification here, which is part of why the following ayah lands as it does.
A verb for gathering something up and selecting it for oneself, used of prophets being singled out. Placing it before the pardon means the choosing was not a reward for having been forgiven.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Repairing rather than replacing was ordinary life. Sandals were restitched, waterskins patched, tents mended where thorns had torn them, and a household's cloth was worked and reworked until it could not hold. The image of two people stitching leaves onto themselves would have read as recognisable and slightly desperate, the gesture of anyone caught out with nothing suitable to hand.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing the covering with leaves occurs twice in the Quran and both times of this same moment, here and in surah 7. It is otherwise a workshop word, used of a cobbler laying one piece of leather over another. The Quran describes the first human embarrassment with the vocabulary of shoe repair.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of the three verbs is the passage's argument. Being chosen comes first, so the restoration is not earned by the repentance that follows it, and guidance comes last, so the person is not simply returned to where he was but sent forward. The plain statement of the fault matters too. Nothing is minimised, which is what makes the recovery meaningful rather than a way of saying it never happened.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same recovery, with words received from his Lord and the turning that followed them.
Narrates the same moment and adds the prayer the two of them made about wronging themselves.
Uses the same verb for choosing, of God selecting whom He wills and guiding whoever turns to Him.

studies.applyIt: Notice which verb comes first. If you are carrying something you think has disqualified you, read the order again: chosen, then pardoned, then guided. Say the three in that sequence once today about your own situation. It is a different sentence from the one most people tell themselves, and it is the one the ayah actually gives.

studies.title: Go Down From It Together
studies.meaning: The sentence is not framed as punishment but as relocation with terms attached. Two are told to descend, then the address widens and hostility is described as a feature of the place they are going to. What follows is the condition of everything after: guidance will come, and whoever follows it is promised two negatives. He will not go astray and he will not suffer, which are exactly the two things the descent seemed to guarantee.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is closing its account of the first human story, and this ayah is the hinge between that story and the situation of everyone reading it. The Meccan audience were being asked to accept that a message had arrived and that following it was the whole of what was required. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah; its position at the end of the narrative carries the weight.

keyTerms.note: A dual imperative, addressed to two, though the sentence immediately widens to many. Commentators discuss the shift, reading it as the descent of two people opening onto the condition of everyone after them.
Stated as something that will come from God rather than be found, and left indefinite. The promise attaches to following what arrives, not to searching successfully for it.
The same word used in the warning six ayat earlier about what leaving the garden would cost. Its return here is the surah cancelling its own threat for anyone who follows guidance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent from high ground to low was a literal movement in Arabian life. Tribes came down from the hills to the valley floors for water and market, and the word for going down carried the sense of arriving in a place where others already were and where disputes had to be managed. Enmity between neighbouring groups was not an idea in that world. It was the standing condition of shared wells and shared grazing.
studies.didYouKnow: The two things promised to whoever follows guidance are stated as denials, and the second of them repeats a word from the warning given six ayat earlier, when leaving the garden was said to lead to suffering. The surah opened with almost the same move, telling the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that the Quran was not sent down to make him wretched.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage reframes the human situation as a place with terms rather than as an exile. Enmity is acknowledged as part of the setting, not denied, and the response offered is not escape but guidance. What is promised is modest and precise: not comfort or success, but not being lost and not being wretched. Everything else that happens on earth is left standing where it is.

crossReferences.why: Gives the warning this ayah answers, that being driven out would lead to suffering.
Gives the same descent and promise, phrased there as no fear upon them and no grief.
Opens this surah with the same word, saying the Quran was not sent down to cause wretchedness.

studies.applyIt: Look at what is actually promised here. Not ease, not protection from other people, only that you will not be lost and will not be wretched. Try holding today to that smaller guarantee. When something goes badly, ask whether it has actually made you lost, or only made you uncomfortable. They are different, and the ayah is careful about which one it covers.

studies.title: A Life Made Narrow
studies.meaning: The consequence named is not poverty and not punishment yet, but constriction. Whoever turns away from the Reminder has a life described as tight, and the commentators offer a range for what that means: anxiety, the torment of the grave, an unquiet heart, a life with no ease in it however much it holds. Then a second consequence, raised blind on the Day, which the next ayat show him protesting.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah is part of the closing address of the Adam narrative, spoken as the two of them are sent down from the garden with a condition attached: whoever follows My guidance will not go astray nor suffer. This is the other half of that sentence. No specific occasion is reported. The surah as a whole was revealed in the years of open hostility in Mecca.

keyTerms.note: A rare word for cramped space, used of a tight dwelling or a hard passage. It describes a life by its dimensions rather than its contents, so wealth does not exclude it.
The verb is built on the word for a side, so it means to present your side rather than your face. It describes a bodily turn and implies awareness: you cannot turn away from what you never saw.

Used here of the Day rather than of this life. The reply given two ayat later matches the punishment to the act, since forgetting is answered with being forgotten and turning the face away with not seeing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Narrowness was a physical experience people knew well. A poor family lived in one room; a caravan route through a gorge closed in on either side; a tent in a sandstorm shrank to the space you could breathe in. The word chosen here carries all of that. It was not an abstract description of unhappiness but the feeling of walls, applied to a life that might look spacious from outside.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the straitened life occurs only once in the Quran. Its rarity is part of why commentators have written so much about it: there is no second usage to fix the meaning, so the range is set by the root and by context. The passage it belongs to also ends the Adam story by turning it into a general condition rather than a single event.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah describes a consequence that arrives inside a life rather than after it, which makes turning away self-punishing rather than merely punishable. That is a claim about how human beings are built: something is missing and its absence is felt as pressure, whether or not it is identified. The blindness on the Day then extends the same logic forward, so the two conditions are one condition seen at two moments.

crossReferences.why: The exact counterpart: hearts settle by the remembrance this ayah describes turning from.
The protest that follows and the answer: you forgot, so today you are forgotten.
Describes a companion assigned to whoever turns blind to the Merciful's reminder.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you feel that low, unplaceable pressure in the chest, the kind with no obvious cause. Before reaching for the phone, try three minutes of something that counts as remembrance for you: a page read slowly, a short phrase repeated, a prayer said properly. Then check whether the pressure is where it was. This ayah is making a testable claim.

studies.title: Though I Once Could See
studies.meaning: A question is asked and answered without any argument between them. The complaint is about a faculty lost, and it is put in the past tense: he was seeing, and now he is not. The reply does not address the eyes at all. It sets the two events side by side using the same word twice, the signs came and were forgotten, and today the same thing happens to him. The correspondence is left to do the explaining.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The exchange follows the description of a life made narrow for whoever turns away from the reminder. Meccan opponents included men of standing who considered themselves clear-sighted and the message obvious nonsense, and the surahs of this period repeatedly answer that self-assessment. No occasion of revelation is reported for these two ayat, which continue the address that began several lines earlier.

keyTerms.note: A word for sight and for insight together, so the complaint can be read two ways at once. He may be protesting about his eyes or about his judgement, and the reply treats both as the same claim.

The surah's recurring verb, used here of a person and earlier of the first human being. Forgetting is presented as something done rather than something suffered, which is why it can be answered in kind.
The passive of the same verb, so the reply uses the questioner's own act as its grammar. Commentators read the being forgotten as being left without attention rather than as God's knowledge failing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blindness was common in Arabia and its consequences were social before they were physical. A blind man could not travel alone, could not read the ground, could not join a raid or guide a caravan, and depended entirely on being remembered by others. Being unseen and being unattended amounted to the same condition. The pairing of blindness with being forgotten described one recognisable state, not two.
studies.didYouKnow: Forms of the verb to forget appear in four separate ayat of this surah, and one of those ayat is here, carrying the active and the passive within a single line. The surah's first use of the verb is Moses saying that his Lord neither errs nor forgets, so the only party exempt from this failing is named early and never contradicted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply establishes a form of consequence that is not additional but reflexive: what happens is what was already being done, returned. That keeps justice from looking arbitrary, since nothing new is introduced at the end. It also identifies the fault precisely. It was not disbelief in the sense of examining a claim and rejecting it, but the signs arriving and being allowed to slip out of attention.

crossReferences.why: States the counterpart at the start of this surah, that God neither goes astray nor forgets.
Uses the same reciprocal logic, saying today We forget you as you forgot this meeting of yours.
Says it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts inside the chests, the reading behind this exchange.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true and important that you knew clearly a year ago and have stopped acting on. Not rejected, just let go of. Write it on a card today and put it where you will keep meeting it. The passage does not describe a decision going wrong. It describes attention quietly moving elsewhere.

studies.title: More Severe And More Lasting
studies.meaning: The case is closed with a general rule and a comparison. Two things are named together: going past limits, and not believing the signs of one's Lord. Commentators note that they are given as a pair rather than as alternatives, so excess and refusal describe one movement. The comparison that ends the line does not say the punishment is worse in kind. It says it is more severe and it lasts, which is a claim about duration first.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes the exchange about being raised without sight and rounds off the surah's account of the last day before it turns to the ruins of earlier peoples. Its listeners could see men prospering in Mecca who had rejected the message outright, and the comparison answers the evidence in front of them. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb for spending or acting past the proper measure. It names the fault as overflow rather than as a specific wrong, which lets one word cover waste, arrogance and cruelty together.
A comparative from a root meaning to bind tightly. It measures intensity as a kind of tightening, which is why it pairs naturally with the word for lasting that follows it.

The surah's own recurring measure. Pharaoh used it of his punishments, the magicians used it of God, and it returns twice more before the surah ends, always to decide between two things by which one remains.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Punishment in Arabia was quick and public. A hand was struck, a man was cast out, a rival tribe was raided and the matter was closed within a season, because nobody had the means to sustain anything longer. Prisons barely existed. A penalty that continued indefinitely was outside the practical experience of the audience, which is why the surah keeps arguing by duration rather than by severity.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for lasting appears seven times in the Quran, and four of those are in this surah. Pharaoh uses it to claim his punishment outlasts God's, the magicians immediately turn it back on him, it settles the comparison here, and a few ayat later it describes the provision of the Prophet's Lord against the wealth of others. One word carries the surah's whole argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a question about visible outcomes with a claim about time. It does not deny that the excessive are doing well, and it does not promise they will stop. Instead it moves the comparison to a scale on which what lasts wins, which is the same move the surah has made three times already. Judgement is presented as duration rather than as reversal.

crossReferences.why: Pharaoh uses the same word earlier in this surah, claiming his own punishment is the more lasting.
The magicians answer him with it, saying God is better and more lasting, two ayat later.
Makes the same comparison plainly, that you prefer this life while the hereafter is better and lasts.

studies.applyIt: Take one decision you are weighing and score it on the surah's measure rather than the usual one. Not which option is better now, but which of them will still be there in ten years, and which of you will. The comparison is uncomfortable on purpose. It is also the only comparison this passage thinks is worth making.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: They Walk In Their Dwellings
studies.meaning: The argument is put as a question about evidence already underfoot. Whole generations ended, and the people being addressed pass through the places where they lived. The detail that does the work is the walking: this is not history read but ground crossed. The second ayah then explains why the same thing has not happened to them, and the reason is not their merit. A word already given and a fixed term are holding the outcome off.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The trade routes north from Mecca ran past abandoned settlements, and the Quran refers to them repeatedly for an audience that had seen them. The community was under pressure and some wanted a decisive judgement on their opponents; this ayah explains the delay without promising it will end soon. No specific occasion of revelation is reported, though the setting is the ordinary Meccan objection about why nothing happens.

keyTerms.note: A word for a span of people living at one time rather than for a period on a calendar. It measures history in populations, so what was destroyed is counted as communities rather than as years.
From a root for sticking fast to something. It occurs twice in the Quran and names an outcome already attached to a case, waiting only for its time rather than for a decision.
Literally something that has been given a name. A term that is named is fixed and known to the one who named it, which is a different claim from saying it is merely far off.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravans out of Mecca passed real ruins. Rock-cut facades stood empty in the north, wells lay silted in the settlements of vanished tribes, and guides pointed them out on the road to Syria. Travellers camped among them because the walls broke the wind. Walking through the dwellings of a finished people was not a metaphor for that audience; it was several nights of an ordinary trading journey.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the inevitable in the second of these ayat occurs twice in the whole Quran, and both places make the same point about a judgement already fixed and merely postponed. The other is at the very end of a long surah about the servants of the Merciful, so the term appears once in the middle of an argument and once as a closing word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Delay is given a reason that is not leniency and not indifference. A word has gone ahead and a term has been named, so what looks like nothing happening is an arrangement rather than an absence. That protects two things at once: the seriousness of the warning, and the reader's ability to trust a God who does not act on demand. It also relocates evidence from argument to landscape.

crossReferences.why: Closes another surah with the same word for what has become binding, after the same kind of refusal.
Describes towns left in ruins and asks whether they travel through the land with hearts that understand.
Gives the same explanation for delay, a word already gone forth from your Lord deciding what was disputed.

studies.applyIt: Look up one place near you that used to be something else: the factory, the cinema, the family shop. Walk past it this week if you can, and let the fact that people organised their whole lives around it land for a moment. The passage is not asking for gloom. It is asking you to read a building as evidence.

studies.title: Before The Sun Rises
studies.meaning: An instruction to endure and an instruction to praise, given as one thing. The times listed are unusually specific: before sunrise, before sunset, during the hours of the night, and at the ends of the day. Commentators connect these to the times of prayer, with some variation in how the list maps onto them. The final word is the surprising one. The purpose given is not reward but that you may be satisfied.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of the surah, after a passage about earlier generations whose ruins the audience walked through and a statement that only an appointed term is holding back the consequence. The instruction to bear what they say is therefore given at a moment of maximum provocation. The commentators report no specific occasion. The ayah that follows tells him not to look at what others have been given.

keyTerms.note: A plural for stretches of time within the night, used of the parts of the darkness rather than fixed hours. The word leaves the timing open and suggests spread rather than a single appointed moment.
Literally the extremities of a thing, as of a limb or a cloth. Applied to the day it names the seams where one part gives way to another, which is where the instruction places the practice.

A verb for being content with something, not for receiving it. Making the reader's own satisfaction the stated purpose is unusual, and the commentators note that it points to a state reached rather than a payment received.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A day in Arabia was measured by the sun and nothing else. There were no clocks, and work, travel and rest were organised around the two edges when the heat broke. Everyone was awake before sunrise; everyone stopped before sunset. Setting the practice at those points did not add hours to a person's day. It attached something to the two moments when the whole settlement was already stirring.
studies.didYouKnow: The last word of the ayah is read in two ways in the recognised recitations, one meaning that you may be satisfied and the other that you may be granted satisfaction. Both are transmitted and both are accepted. Commentators treat the pair as complementary rather than competing, since one names the state and the other names its source.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Praise is offered as the answer to being insulted, which is not the obvious pairing. The passage does not tell him to defend himself, to correct the record, or even to wait; it tells him to fill the day with something else at fixed points. That treats endurance as a matter of what occupies the hours rather than of how much strength is summoned. And the promised outcome is contentment, which is described as a consequence of the practice rather than of the situation changing.

crossReferences.why: Names almost the same times for praise, before sunrise and before setting.
Sets out the times of prayer with the night vigil as an addition.
Two ayat later, the same instruction extended to the household.

studies.applyIt: Take the two edges this ayah names and put something in each of them for one week: three minutes before you look at your phone in the morning, three minutes before you eat in the evening. The same words both times. The instruction ties patience to a schedule rather than to willpower, which is why it is worth trying as a schedule.

studies.title: Splendour And What Is Lasting
studies.meaning: Three additions make this more than a warning against envy. What others have been given is called the bloom of this life, a word for a flower at its brightest and briefest. Then a purpose is stated for the giving itself: it is a test for them, which reframes what looks like favour. And the closing comparison is doubled, better and more lasting, so the argument turns on quality and duration rather than on quantity.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the closing instructions of the surah, immediately after the command to praise at the edges of the day and immediately before the command to tell the household to pray. The classical sources report no specific occasion. The community around the message included many with nothing, while the men rejecting it held the caravan shares, the water rights and the offices of the sanctuary.

keyTerms.note: The word for a flower at its most brilliant, and by extension the shine on a thing. It carries the brevity with the beauty, since nobody expects a blossom to hold.
From a root meaning to put metal in fire to separate it from its ore. The word for testing in Arabic is a smelting word, so the giving is described as heat applied rather than as reward.
A comparative from the verb to remain. Pairing it with better means the two provisions are not being ranked by size at all; one simply outlasts the other, which decides the comparison.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Spring in Arabia was short and spectacular. After winter rain the wadis filled with flowers for a few weeks, and then the heat took all of it back to stone and dust. Herders moved to catch that window and knew exactly how long it lasted. Choosing the word for blossom to describe another man's wealth used the one natural event everybody had watched arrive and disappear.
studies.didYouKnow: A near-identical instruction appears in an earlier surah, with the same opening verb and the same object. The difference is what each adds: the earlier one follows with gentleness towards believers, this one with the purpose of the test and the comparison of provisions. Reading them together shows the Quran developing an instruction across chapters rather than repeating it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah reassigns what a person is looking at. Abundance in another's hands is not evidence of divine approval; it is described as material for a test whose result is not yet in. That removes the sting from the comparison without denying the difference. And the counter-offer is not that you will get the same later. It is a different provision, named as your Lord's, which is a claim about the source rather than about the amount.

crossReferences.why: The earlier form of the same instruction, closing on gentleness rather than on provision.
Warns against admiring the wealth and children of others, and gives a reason.
A crowd envies a man's display, and those given knowledge answer them.

studies.applyIt: Pick the account or the person whose life you compare yourself to most, and mute them for a week. Not unfollow, not a speech about it: mute. Then notice on day five what you have been thinking about instead. The ayah treats the looking as the mechanism, which means the intervention is on the looking rather than on the feeling.

studies.title: We Ask No Provision Of You
studies.meaning: Three things are set beside each other and the order matters. The household is to be called to prayer, and the one calling them is told to hold to it himself with an intensified form of patience. Then, without transition, the subject changes to money: no provision is being asked of him, and he is the one being provided for. Commentators read the join as answering the anxiety that makes people trade attention to prayer for attention to income.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a period when the small community's means were genuinely reduced and some families faced real hardship for their allegiance. The instruction is addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about his own household, and follows immediately on the warning not to look longingly at what others have been given. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: An intensified form of the ordinary verb for patience, used only three times in the Quran. It suggests effort sustained against resistance rather than endurance of something that simply happens to you.
What is allotted to a creature to live on, not what is earned. The word's framing is why the sentence can move from prayer to income without changing the subject.
What follows on the heels of something, from a root for a heel. It names the last phase of a matter, so the claim is about how things finish rather than how they look while running.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan household ran on the trading season. Two caravans a year, one to Yemen and one to Syria, carried the capital that fed a family through the months between, and a man's mornings and evenings were spent arranging credit, animals and partners. Time set aside daily, at fixed hours, for something that produced no return was a visible economic choice, and everyone around him could see it being made.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensified form of the verb for patience used here occurs three times in the whole Quran. One is this instruction, one is an address about worshipping the Lord of the heavens and holding patiently to that worship, and one is the command given about the she-camel sent as a test to an earlier people. All three attach patience to something ongoing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a fear rather than issuing an argument. Attention given to prayer is not framed as a sacrifice to be compensated later; the sentence simply removes the premise by saying that provision was never the reader's to generate. It also puts the one instructing others under the same instruction, which prevents the calling of a household from becoming a matter of authority rather than of shared practice.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same intensified verb for patience, there about holding to the worship of the Lord of all things.
States the same point about provision plainly, that God is the Provider and asks no sustenance from anyone.
Comes immediately before, warning against straining the eyes towards what others have been given.

studies.applyIt: Notice the join in this ayah between attention and income. Pick one hour this week that you would normally spend earning or worrying about earning, and give it to your household instead, doing something unhurried together. Do not calculate the cost of it. The whole point of the second half of the ayah is that the calculation was never yours to make.

studies.title: In The Earlier Scriptures
studies.meaning: A demand is quoted and answered with a question rather than a sign. They want something brought to them from his Lord, and the reply points at what has already reached them: the clear evidence contained in the earlier books. Commentators read this as directing them to the record of previous peoples that the surah has just spent eighty ayat retelling. The answer refuses the terms of the request without dismissing the questioners.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Demands for a spectacular sign are reported repeatedly from this period, and the Quran's usual response is to decline them and point to what has been given. The Meccan audience knew of Jewish and Christian scriptures through traders and through the communities of Yathrib and the north, so an appeal to earlier books was not an appeal to something unavailable. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The same word the Quran uses for its own verses and for signs in nature. The demand asks for one kind while the reply points at another, and the ambiguity is in the word itself.
A word from the legal and commercial vocabulary of the time, used for the proof a claimant brings. It sets the exchange in terms of evidence already submitted rather than of wonders still owed.
Sheets or leaves that carry writing. The plural describes earlier revelation as physical documents, which is how the argument treats them: as a record available to be consulted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was largely an oral town, but written documents carried a particular authority within it. Treaties were inscribed and hung in the sanctuary, debts and caravan shares were recorded, and the few men who could read held a distinct standing. Jews and Christians on the trade routes were known as people who kept books. Pointing to written scripture invoked exactly that authority in an argument conducted mostly by speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for the earlier scriptures occurs twice in the whole Quran. The other is near the end of a very short surah, where the same expression closes a passage by naming two of those earlier books. In both places the phrase does the same work, appealing past the present dispute to a record that the audience already accepted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply declines to treat faith as a transaction in which a sign is purchased by a demand. What it offers instead is continuity: this message is not a new claim requiring fresh proof but the latest instance of something already documented. That reframing also protects the questioners from their own request, since the surah has just shown at length what happened to a people who saw signs and were unchanged by them.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase for the earlier scriptures and names two of them at the close of a short surah.
Answers the same demand, saying that even a sign brought would not make them believe.
Meets the identical request by asking whether the book recited to them is not itself sufficient.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what would actually change your mind about something you are unsure of, and then whether you would accept it if it arrived. Most people find the second answer is no. That is the mechanism this ayah is describing, and noticing it in a small matter is the only reliable way to recognise it in a large one.

studies.title: Everyone Is Waiting
studies.meaning: An objection is answered before it is made. Had judgement come without a messenger, they would have had a complaint, and the Quran states their complaint for them in their own words, including the humiliation they would have wanted to avoid. That closes the argument about signs. Then the surah ends by handing the dispute over to time. Everybody is waiting, so wait, and the last word is left as a question that only the outcome will settle.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These are the final two ayat of the surah, closing an argument that has run since the demand for a miracle. The community was small and its opponents confident, and the instruction to wait was addressed to people who could see no near prospect of vindication. No specific occasion of revelation is reported. The surah ends without resolving the confrontation it describes.

keyTerms.note: A waiting that watches for an outcome, used elsewhere of people watching to see which way a conflict turns. It is applied here to both sides at once, which is what makes the instruction sting.
This word occurs only here. It describes a path that is level and without deviation, so the closing question is about which road is straight rather than about who is stronger.
The reflexive form for taking up guidance and keeping it, the same verb used earlier in this surah as the last of four conditions for forgiveness. It is the final word of the surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Waiting was a strategy in Arabia, not a mood. Tribes uncommitted in a quarrel watched to see which side would prevail before declaring themselves, and the word for it carried that political sense. Caravans waited out a season, poets waited for the fairs, families waited for a raid's outcome before arranging marriages. To be told to wait was to be placed in a familiar and uncomfortable position.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah closes on the verb for being rightly guided, and the same verb appeared earlier as the last of the four things named for one who repents, believes and acts well and then stays guided. The word for the level path in the final line occurs nowhere else in the Quran, so the surah ends with a term used only once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing move refuses to force the question. Both sides are described as waiting, which grants the opponents a position rather than caricaturing them, and the outcome is left to be known rather than asserted. The earlier ayah does something equally careful: it takes an excuse that was never made and answers it, establishing that no one will be able to say afterwards that they were judged without warning.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same closing verb earlier in this surah as the last of four steps for the one who repents.
Gives the same argument, that a disaster without a messenger would have produced exactly this complaint.
Ends a similar exchange with the instruction to wait, since the ones addressed are waiting too.

studies.applyIt: The surah does not end with a proof. It ends with an instruction to keep going while the matter is unsettled, which is where most of life is lived. Take one thing you are waiting on, and today do the next small piece of your part in it without asking for a sign first. That is what the last line is describing.
